At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 15.20 to 7.00 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73 % 33.73\% to 72.96 % 72.96\% . Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory. Figure 1: T2-z for Test-Time Environment Latent Optimization. (a) Given the same observation and action, T2-z directly optimizes environment latents to capture different environmental conditions ( e.g., ball mass), leading the world model to predict different outcomes. (b) Without knowing how many factors exist or what they represent, PCA of the learned environment latents reveals a two-dimensional structure that closely reflects the underlying factor distribution. (c) We evaluate T2-z on real-world robotic tasks spanning diverse unobserved environmental factors. (d) Across diverse visual scenes, the learned latents reveal a unified structure that reflects the same underlying environmental factor without being entangled with visual appearance. 1 Introduction What a robot observes is insufficient to determine how the world will respond. Beneath visually similar scene configurations reside hidden environmental factors, such as friction, mass distribution, and unobserved human-defined interaction rules, that can fundamentally alter the consequences of the same action ( fig. 1 (a)). Such factors are often revealed only through interaction with the target environments, as their influence becomes observable through the outcomes they induce. Even with a deterministic evaluator, the same harness can lead a stochastic executor to different solutions. An observed score therefore mixes the quality of a proposed procedure with downstream sampling variability. Our RLOO-based update [ 2 , 25 ] must assign credit under this indirect feedback while accounting for shrinking absolute gains and an objective that retains the best discovery rather than the average attempt. \para Reward. Recent work [ 77 , 72 , 65 ] on AI for scientific discovery formulates each task as an exploration for

xecutor sampling variability. We develop a discovery-oriented RLOO-based update [ 25 , 2 ] with gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages without variance normalization [ 34 ] , max-sharpening [ 54 , 6 ] , and filtering of uninformative groups [ 74 ] , designed to limit noise amplification while accommodating heterogeneous reward scales and best-of-group selection. Second, harness optimization must guard against reward hacking and information leakage . Higher evaluator scores do not necessarily reflect better solutions: an agent may exploit flaws in the evaluation process [ 26 , 39 ] or use information unavailable under the intended task protocol [ 23 ] . We therefore design a new critic component to address this challenge. Figure 3: Where is test-time reward retained? (a) Executor weights : the policy that solves the task is also the policy being trained [ 77 , 65 ] . (b) Proposer context : the executor stays frozen and a fixed proposer re-reads an archive or harness accumulated over rounds [ 42 , 58 , 29 ] . (c) Proposer weights (ours) : a separate proposer is trained to write complete harnesses for a frozen executor, so adaptation is amortized into weights while remaining expressed as inspectable artifacts. We evaluate HarnessTTT on fourteen discovery problems spanning mathematical constructions [ 42 , 14 ] , systems benchmarks [ 9 ] , GPU kernels [ 77 ] , heuristic programming contests [ 4 , 22 ] , astrodynamics, and biology. With a frozen Qwen3.5-9B executor [ 49 ] , HarnessTTT improves on OpenEvolve with the same executor on all eleven benchmark tasks and holds the best open-weight sub-10B result on nine, ahead of the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B [ 30 ] on every task by up to 91.7 % 91.7\% . We first formulate the discovery objective, then describe the harness representation, proposer update, iterative search, and validation protocol. \para Problem formulation and framework overview. A task τ \tau provides a description d τ d_{\tau} , a seed program x 0 x_{0} with a marked editable region, and a black-box evaluator m τ m_{\tau} ; the seed program and evaluator are taken from Lee et al. [30] . Each rollout may call the evaluator at most B B times. An agent pairs a frozen language-model executor M 0 M_{0} with an executable harness H H that governs how M 0 M_{0} interacts with the task. Each outer round starts from a search state: the incumbent program x ⋆ x^{\star} (the best found so far, initially x 0 x_{0} ) with score b τ = m τ ​ ( x ⋆ ) b_{\tau}=m_{\tau}(x^{\star}) , the incumbent harness H ⋆ H^{\star} , and an experience digest D D . Given this context, the proposer π ϕ \pi_{\phi} samples K K harness specifications. Each round keeps a single incumbent harness H ⋆ H^{\star} , but proposals are dealt round-robin between H ⋆ H^{\star} and one diversity-preserving runner-up parent: the best candidate within 2% of the top score that adds a new component, or else the second-highest scorer. This keeps components from non-winning candidates alive for another round [ 1 , 81 ] . In the first round all K K proposals share the initial harness. Each specification is merged into its parent, validated, and compiled into a candidate harness H k H_{k} ; all candidates start from the same program x ⋆ x^{\star} . Only the proposer’s LoRA adapter ϕ \phi is trained [ 19 ] ; M 0 M_{0} is never updated. A rollout of M 0 M_{0} under H k H_{k} edits the program and calls the evaluator on programs x k , 1 , … , x k , T x_{k,1},\dots,x_{k,T} ( T ≤ B T\leq B ); its score is the best valid score it finds, s k = max t ≤ T ⁡ m τ ​ ( x k , t ) s_{k}=\max_{t\leq T}m_{\tau}(x_{k,t}) , where invalid programs are skipped and a rollout without any valid program counts as failed. We fix the harnesses learned with Qwen3.5-9B (the evolved harness ) and swap the executor for GLM-5.2, GLM-5.1 [ 15 ] , GPT-5.3 [ 44 ] , Qwen-235B [ 69 ] , or GPT-OSS-120B [ 43 ] , without using any of their outcomes to train the proposer. For each executor, OpenEvolve [ 58 ] runs 48 iterations from the initial or the evolved harness under identical settings, and NexAU [ 41 ] records tool use over three decode seeds. The evolved harness raises the eleven-task mean normalized score on all five executors by + 1.2 +1.2 to + 13.4 +13.4 points ( + 5.4 +5.4 on average; Figure 7 ). The gains track custom-tool use: Qwen-235B calls the generated tools most often (19.9 attempts per 100 turns) and gains the most ( + 13.4 +13.4 ), followed by GPT-5.3 (9.9; + 5.7 +5.7 ). The harness thus carries a reusable search procedure that other executors can execute, without proposer retraining or executor-weight updates; with one search seed per executor, these gains are descriptive point estimates. Right : mean normalized score after 48 OpenEvolve iterations from the initial versus the evolved harness (one search seed). TDAL uses the Hellinger distance between hit probabilities for unmeasured candidates before and after an experiment to weight successor value, and reuses measured outcomes through leave-batch-out (LBO) to construct virtual transitions and alleviate training data scarcity. Across eight public screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations under varied experimental configurations, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods and ranks first on four tasks, demonstrating its adaptability across response landscapes. 1 Introduction Large-scale perturbational screens deepen the understanding of disease mechanisms and help validate therapeutic targets ( Schmidt et al., 2022 ; Zhuang et al., 2019 ; Sanchez et al., 2021 ) . The human genome comprises nearly 20,000 single-gene candidates, roughly 200 million pairs, and one trillion triples in terms of perturbation combinations. The costs of testing each perturbation and measuring its phenotype make exhaustive screening infeasible ( Mehrjou et al., 2022 ; Pacchiano et al., 2023 ) . Closed-loop systems have shown that model-guided experiment selection can improve biological discovery under limited resources ( Xu et al., 2026 ; DeMeo et al., 2025 ) . It is thus important to develop strategies that maximize cumulative discoveries within a fixed experimental budget. Active learning addresses this challenge by iteratively fitting a surrogate model to measured outcomes and using an acquisition function to select subsequent experiments (Figure 1 a). GeneDisco evaluates active learning methods for perturbation screening and reports substantial variation in their performance across experimental settings ( Mehrjou et al., 2022 ) . Existing methods employ different selection criteria to guide perturbation discovery. OAE ( Pacchiano et al., 2023 ) seeks near-optimal perturbations, DiscoBAX ( Lyle et al., 2023 ) considers response strength and mechanistic diversity, and Probability-of-Hit (PoH) ( Rubbi et al., 2026 ) prioritizes perturbations that exceed a predefined phenotypic threshold. Recent approaches also incorporate language model agents or biological priors into experiment selection ( Roohani et al., 2025 ; Hao et al.

Methods include BALD, which uses information gain ( Houlsby et al., 2011 ) , CoreSet, which emphasizes geometric coverage ( Sener and Savarese, 2018 ) , and BADGE, which combines uncertainty and diversity ( Ash et al., 2020 ) . For discovery, active search ( Garnett et al., 2012 ) , ENS ( Jiang et al., 2017 ) , and its batch extension ( Jiang et al., 2018 ) evaluate future hits within the budget. IDS ( Xu et al., 2022 ) balances instantaneous regret and information gain to increase cumulative response. These methods adapt sampling to observations but retain predefined acquisition functions. Other approaches learn acquisition functions from data. Learning Active Learning predicts expected error reduction ( Konyushkova et al., 2017 ) . MetaBO trains acquisition functions through reinforcement learning across tasks ( Volpp et al., 2020 ) . Amortized active search trains a neural network to imitate ENS selections ( Nguyen et al., 2024 ) . In molecular discovery, GLARE updates its selection policy online using measured activity labels ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , while Zhang et al. (2026) learn a policy to identify the optimal molecule. SOFisher uses Double DQN to select spatial-omics fields of view ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Our code will be made publicly available. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents interact with environments by interpreting observations and taking actions to accomplish tasks. Long-horizon tasks require them to sustain progress under incomplete observations, where poor decisions can lead to repeated failures or wasted interactions. Building agents that make reliable decisions over extended interactions therefore remains a central challenge. Prior work improves interactive decision making in several complementary ways. ReAct interleaves reasoning with environment feedback ( Yao et al., 2023b ) , but commits to a single proposed action at each step, which may miss useful alternatives. Search-based methods instead explore multiple reasoning or action paths at inference time ( Yao et al., 2023a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Hao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , but their cost grows with the breadth and depth of the search. A separate line improves agents through retrieved reflections and trajectory-derived action advantages ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2026a ) . These directions motivate exploring a few alternatives before acting, without executing them, together with experience gathered through interaction. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our current dual-branch adaptation relies on retrieved textual experience while keeping model parameters frozen. More capable mechanisms for improving world model accuracy and adapting to changing dynamics remain an important direction for future work. Second, evaluating multiple candidates requires additional world model and evaluator calls at test time. This increases inference latency and cost as the candidate set grows, motivating more computationally efficient ways to obtain useful candidate comparisons. Ethical considerations. Our experiments are conducted entirely in text-based simulated environments and involve no human subjects or personal data. If such an agent were deployed in real environments, inaccurate world model predictions could lead to unsafe actions, so human oversight would be needed.
